sections.html:
Greene County's largest city, Beavercreek, lies roughly five miles east of downtown Dayton, which puts many of its houses within an easy commute of Dayton employers. The 2025 population estimate is 48,134, about 3% above the 2020 count of 46,549.

Owners live in most of the homes here. The median home value is $279,600 and the median rent is $1,457. The city has 19,453 households averaging 2.39 people, and typical monthly owner costs run $1,837 with a mortgage and $838 without. Renters fill a bit more than a quarter of occupied homes, so investors and tenants round out the buyer pool.

Part of Beavercreek Township became a city in February 1980, absorbing the old communities of Alpha, Knollwood, most of New Germany and Zimmerman. An older deed may use one of those names. Your title company cares more about the legal description and parcel number than the neighborhood label.

With a long repair list, you can ask a direct buyer for an as-is offer and skip the renovation. A cash sale also skips the lender appraisal and the repair requests that often follow a buyer's inspection.

sections.h2: Permits and registrations that come up at sale
sections.html:
Permits split between the city and the county. The city's Planning and Development Department issues zoning permits, and Greene County Building Regulation handles building, plumbing, electrical and HVAC permits. Match each past project to its permit now, and you will find open work before a buyer's inspector does.

Permit Beavercreek requires for common residential projects
ProjectPermit or office
New house, addition or attached garageResidential Zoning Permit
DeckResidential Zoning Permit
Swimming poolSwimming Pool Permit
Shed or detached garage, propane tankAccessory Structure Permit
Fence or retaining wallFence Permit
Interior remodel such as wall removal or a finished basementGreene County Building Regulation, no zoning permit
Abandoned, foreclosure or vacant propertyRegistration Application

Zoning permits are not required for interior remodeling, at-grade patios, garage sales or driveways. You can apply in the online permit center or hand a printed form to staff at City Hall on Research Park Drive. If the house is vacant, ask the planning office whether the registration rule applies to it.

  • Greene County Building Regulation, at 667 Dayton-Xenia Road in Xenia, issues building, plumbing, electrical and HVAC permits.
  • Greene County Public Health, at 360 Wilson Drive in Xenia, is the contact for health department questions.
  • Greene County Sanitary Engineering, at the Dayton-Xenia Road address, handles sewer questions.
  • The Beavercreek Fire Department is at 851 N. Orchard Lane.

sections.h2: Renting your house by the night
sections.html:
Short-term rentals are allowed with a city license. Ordinance 23-15 and Chapter 117 of the city code require every owner to apply through the Online Permit Center before renting for fewer than thirty consecutive days. A license lasts two years and has to be renewed.

  • The application lists the location, where the unit will be advertised, bedrooms, maximum occupants, parking and emergency contacts.
  • Renters must be at least 25 years old, and owners must hand them house rules, noise rules and emergency details.
  • The city's 3% hotel, motel and short-term rental tax is filed quarterly, even for quarters with no rentals.

If an HOA governs your street, read its covenants before you advertise. If your house has run as a rental, tell buyers about the license and the tax filings, and ask the planning office whether a new owner must file a fresh application.

sections.h2: How Greene County processes a deed
sections.html:
Transfer of the deed runs through the Greene County Auditor, and the recorder files it once the auditor signs off. The auditor requires a completed Real Property Conveyance Statement of Value and Receipt (form DTE 100), and the grantor's name must match how the grantor took title in the previous deed. The county map department approves the deed before it reaches the auditor, and land in the farmland tax program needs the DTE 101 statement.

Expect two charges: fifty cents per parcel in transfer tax, plus a conveyance fee of $2 for every thousand dollars of sale price, rounded up to the nearest $100. The county runs an online calculator so you can see the amount for your sale.

The recorder also wants a complete legal description with the parcel number, a prepared-by statement, the prior deed reference and a notarial acknowledgment. A title company normally assembles all of this at closing, but it is worth confirming your name is spelled the same way on every document.

The county auditor appraises each parcel at fair market value every six years and updates values every three. The auditor's office is at 69 Greene Street in Xenia, and its appraisers will talk through a valuation or help you start an appeal. Property taxes fund schools, public safety, roads, libraries and parks.

Due dates shift with state changes. In one recent year, the House Bill 186 inflation cap credit delayed second-half bills in Greene County. For your own closing year, ask the treasurer for the schedule, and have the title company prorate the tax between you and the buyer so each side pays for the months they own the house.

If taxes are owed when you sell, the title company pays them out of your proceeds at closing, so ask for a payoff figure early. Carry your latest tax bill, a copy of your deed, and a recent mortgage statement into your first call with the title company.

The Beavercreek City School District runs one preschool, six elementary schools, two middle schools, a Freshman School and Beavercreek High School. Beavercreek's parks department looks after 24 parks and properties, and Beavercreek Station is a hub on Creekside Trail, which runs from Xenia to Eastwood MetroPark in Dayton. The Greater Dayton Regional Transit Authority runs bus service in the city.

Buyers like these amenities. If you sell as is, ask the buyer to state in writing that repairs are theirs, and keep a copy of any inspection report you ordered. A sensible order of operations is permits first, deed paperwork second, a tax proration estimate third, and only then a side by side look at what each offer nets you. A cash buyer can usually pick a closing date that fits your move, which helps if you are relocating for work in the Dayton area. At the table you sign the deed in front of a notary, hand over the keys, and the title company sends your proceeds once the transfer goes through. If any permit sits unfinished, finishing it first usually costs less than a price cut later.

faqs.q: Do I need a city permit to sell a house in Beavercreek?
faqs.a: No permit is needed to sell. Check for open permits on past work, though, since decks, pools, fences and sheds need zoning permits and the county handles building, plumbing, electrical and HVAC permits.

faqs.q: What fees does Greene County charge on a deed?
faqs.a: A transfer tax of fifty cents per parcel and a conveyance fee of $2 per thousand dollars of the sale price, rounded up to the nearest $100. The county's online calculator shows the amount for your sale.

faqs.q: Can a Beavercreek short-term rental license pass to a buyer?
faqs.a: Ask the planning office. Licenses last two years and go to the owner who applies, so a new owner may need to file a new application through the Online Permit Center.

faqs.q: When are Greene County taxes due?
faqs.a: Dates are set each year and can move after state changes such as House Bill 186. Ask the Greene County Treasurer for the schedule that matches your closing.

faqs.q: What must I disclose when I sell my Beavercreek home?
faqs.a: Complete the Ohio property disclosure form if the home has up to four units. ORC 5302.30 lists exceptions such as estate sales and transfers to relatives, and the signed deed must be acknowledged before a notary under ORC 5301.01.
